w: For two thousand years this was Cordoba's only crossing of the Guadalquivir, so locals just call it the Old Bridge. Built by the Romans in the 1st century, rebuilt by the Arabs in the 8th, it carried every traveller and mule train into the city until a new bridge finally took the load in the mid-20th century.
s: Cordoba's only river crossing for two thousand years
_facts: Roman bridge originally built early 1st century AD across the Guadalquivir
Known locally as the Old Bridge - the city's only bridge for two thousand years, until the San Rafael Bridge in the mid-20th century
Most of the present structure dates from Arab reconstruction in the 8th century
Declared a Bien de Interes Cultural in 1931; part of the historic centre, a World Heritage Site since 1984

w: Isabella and Ferdinand ran their Reconquista campaigns from here, plotting the fall of Granada amid Mudejar-inspired gardens. Alfonso XI built it in 1328 over a Roman governor's residence and the old Umayyad palace - fortress-like outside, splendid within. Part of the old city's World Heritage listing since 1994.
s: Where Isabella and Ferdinand planned the fall of Granada
_facts: Medieval alcazar built on the site of the Islamic-era Umayyad Alcazar, the Roman governor's residence and the Customs
Construction ordered by King Alfonso XI of Castile in 1328
Served as one of the primary residences of Isabella I of Castile and Ferdinand II of Aragon
Sober military exterior, Mudejar-inspired gardens and courtyards inside; Cultural Interest Heritage since 1931; part of the Historic Centre of Cordoba, a World Heritage Site since 1994

w: A fortified gate of Islamic origin in Cordoba's historic centre, the Torre de la Calahorra is easy to walk past next to the city's showier monuments - squat, thick-walled, unmistakably Moorish, and still standing sentinel over the old quarter it once helped defend.
s: A squat Moorish gate tower, easy to overlook
_facts: Fortified gate in the historic centre of Cordoba
The edifice is of Islamic origin

w: Barely bigger than a living room, this Mudejar chamber in the old Juderia was built in 1315 - so small historians debate whether it was a private synagogue, a study house, or a guild's workroom first. Used until the 1492 expulsion, then deconsecrated for centuries, restored and reopened in 1985 as a Jewish museum.
s: One of Spain's last surviving medieval synagogues
_facts: Historic former synagogue at 20 Calle de los Judios in the Jewish Quarter, completed 1315, Mudejar design attributed to Isaac Makheb
Small size suggests it may have been a private synagogue, a yeshiva or study house, or a guild's workroom before conversion
Used as a synagogue until the 1492 expulsion, then used for profane purposes
Restored and reopened in 1985 as a Jewish museum; added to the list of Spanish Cultural Heritage monuments in 1885

w: Its name means Tower of the Wrongly Dead Woman - legend says a husband killed his wife here after a false accusation of adultery, and the name stuck long after the truth stopped mattering. Henry III built the real tower in 1406 over an older Almohad structure, then later used it to jail disgraced nobles.
s: Named for a wife wrongly killed, or so legend says
_facts: Gate tower of the Axerquia wall, built 1406-1408 by order of King Henry III of Castile over a pre-existing Almohad structure
Built to defend the gates of Rincon and Colodro; later used as a prison for nobles
Octagonal plan with an annexed arch
Name means 'Tower of the Wrongly Dead Woman', from a legend of a woman killed there by her husband after a false accusation of adultery

w: A stone waterwheel wedged on the Guadalquivir between the Roman bridge and the Alcazar's walls, its exact age nobody can pin down - most credit the Islamic era, though the truth is lost. It's one of several historic mills that once worked this stretch of river, still standing when the others are gone.
s: A medieval waterwheel of uncertain age, still standing
_facts: Medieval noria (waterwheel) on the Guadalquivir River in the historic centre of Cordoba
One of several historic watermills of Cordoba, located close to the Roman Bridge and the Christian Alcazar
Commonly believed to date from the Islamic era, though its exact origins are uncertain

w: These stables border the Guadalquivir in Cordoba's historic centre and once housed the finest stallions and mares of the royal stud - the working line behind the Andalusian horse, one of Spain's most celebrated breeds, raised here under royal patronage in the shadow of the Alcazar next door.
s: Where the Andalusian horse breed was raised for royalty
_facts: Set of stables in Cordoba's historic centre, bordering the Guadalquivir
Housed the best stallions and mares of the royal stud breed, the Andalusian horse

w: Stretching two and a half kilometres when whole, these are the defensive walls the Romans threw up the moment they took Corduba in 206 BC - the skeleton the whole old town still hangs on. What survives is patchy, but it's original enough to share the historic centre's World Heritage listing since 1984.
s: Roman defences from 206 BC, still framing the old town
_facts: Ancient Roman defensive walls of the Roman colonia of Corduba, stretching 2,650 metres
Built after the Romans captured the city in 206 BC
Surviving sections form part of the historic centre of Cordoba, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1984

w: A Renaissance gate raised in the 16th century to mark a royal visit from Philip II, built on the exact spot where Roman gates once stood, linking the city to its bridge and the old Via Augusta beyond. Grouped with that bridge and the Calahorra tower as a single protected monument since 1931.
s: A Renaissance gate on a two-thousand-year-old Roman site
_facts: Renaissance gate built in the 16th century to commemorate a visit by King Philip II
Located on the site of previous Roman gates, linking the city to the Roman bridge and the Via Augusta
Since 1931, declared a Bien de Interes Cultural together with the Roman bridge and the Calahorra tower; part of the historic centre, a World Heritage Site since 1984

w: Workers expanding City Hall in the 1950s hit stone columns and found Cordoba's grandest Roman temple - a 32-metre Corinthian giant begun under Claudius and finished forty years later under Domitian, likely built for the imperial cult. The only one of the city's Roman temples ever confirmed by excavation.
s: A Roman temple City Hall workers stumbled onto by accident
_facts: Discovered in the 1950s during the expansion of Cordoba's City Hall
Pseudoperipteral, hexastyle, Corinthian-order temple, 32 by 16 metres
Construction began under Emperor Claudius (41-54 AD) and finished about 40 years later under Domitian
Presumably dedicated to the imperial cult; the only one of the city's Roman temples confirmed by excavation

w: The state-owned archaeological museum for a city that keeps turning up more of its own past - Roman remains, Islamic-era finds, medieval fragments - all filed under one roof by Andalusia's Ministry of Culture. A tidy custodian for a famously layered city.
s: The keeper of Cordoba's endlessly resurfacing past
_facts: Archaeological and Ethnological Museum of Cordoba
Owned by the Spanish State, management transferred to the Ministry of Culture of the Junta of Andalusia

w: Franco built this mosque during the Civil War as a thank-you gift to the Muslim soldiers who fought for him - reportedly Spain's first modern mosque, and a strange footnote in a city built by Islamic rule and then reconquered from it. It served decades as an Islamic library before finally reopening for prayer in 1992.
s: Franco's wartime mosque, built for his Muslim soldiers
_facts: Built during the Spanish Civil War as a gift for General Franco's Muslim soldiers
Considered Spain's first modern mosque
Served 1950 to the early 1990s as a specialized library on Islam
Reopened as a mosque in 1992 after Cordoba's Muslim community petitioned the municipal government

w: Wander the tangle of Deanes, Manriquez and Calle de los Judios and you're walking the old Juderia, where Cordoba's Jewish community lived for five centuries. Tucked just northeast of the Mezquita, its streets are part of the historic centre named a World Heritage Site in 1994.
s: The old Jewish quarter, streets barely changed in centuries
_facts: Area where Jews lived in Cordoba between the 10th and 15th centuries
Located in the historic centre, northeast of the Mosque-Cathedral, along the streets Deanes, Manriquez, Tomas Conde, Judios, Almanzor and Romero
Part of the historic centre of Cordoba, named a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1994

w: A king built this church to house his own tomb - Alfonso XI founded it in 1343 and today lies here beside his father Ferdinand IV, royal graves inside Cordoba's old city walls. The Jesuits ran it for centuries after, a Catholic church built, quite literally, as a royal mausoleum.
s: Built by a king, to hold his own grave
_facts: Royal Collegiate Church of Saint Hippolytus, founded 1343 at the initiative of King Alfonso XI of Castile
Later granted in perpetuity to the Society of Jesus
Contains the tombs of King Ferdinand IV and his son Alfonso XI

w: Buried under a public garden until 1993, this cylindrical Roman tomb once marked the road out of the city toward Hispalis - modern Seville. Its design echoes mausoleums back in Rome itself, unusual enough in Roman Iberia that archaeologists suspect an Italian architect and a very wealthy family footing the bill.
s: A Roman millionaire's tomb, buried under a park until 1993
_facts: Cylindrical Roman funerary monument in the Jardines de la Victoria, built in the 1st century AD
Discovered in 1993 during archaeological excavations
Unusual for Roman Iberia, its design suggests an Italian architect and a wealthy owner
Located near the road that connected the city to Hispalis (Seville), exiting via the western gate Puerta de Gallegos

w: Cervantes namechecked this square's old inn in Don Quixote, and the joke was pointed - Plaza del Potro had a reputation for brothels and rough trade. Today it's tamer: a 1577 fountain topped by a rearing colt, the city's Museum of Fine Arts on one side, and the inn Posada del Potro still standing on the other.
s: The square Cervantes joked about in Don Quixote
_facts: Rectangular public square with a Renaissance fountain from 1577, topped by a figure of a rearing colt (potro)
Posada del Potro, an inn overlooking the square, is mentioned by Cervantes in Don Quixote
The city's Museum of Fine Arts and the Julio Romero de Torres Museum also overlook the square
A monument to the Triumph of the Archangel Raphael stands at the other end, since 1924

w: Three faiths stacked on top of each other here: a Visigothic church, then a mosque, then this - one of twelve churches Ferdinand III ordered built after conquering Cordoba in 1236. The old minaret got a Renaissance cap and kept ringing as a bell tower; 14th-century paintings of Christ's life still cover the apse.
s: A minaret turned bell tower, over a mosque, over a church
_facts: One of twelve churches commissioned by King Ferdinand III after the conquest of Cordoba in 1236, built around 1244-1300
Occupies the site of a pre-existing Islamic mosque, itself built over a Visigothic church
The Islamic minaret was converted into a Renaissance bell tower by Hernan Ruiz the Younger
Apse holds 14th-century paintings depicting scenes from the Life of Jesus
